regions.name: Western Pacific warm pool
regions.why: The tropical atmosphere above the warmest ocean on Earth, from the surface to the tropopause.

T2M.label: Air temperature
T2M.simple: How warm the air is 2 metres above the ground — what a thermometer in the shade shows.

TS.label: Surface temperature
TS.simple: The temperature of the surface itself — soil, rock, sea water or ice — which can be much hotter or colder than the air above it.

TROPT.label: Tropopause temperature
TROPT.simple: The temperature at the tropopause, the ceiling of the weather layer of the atmosphere: about 8 km up near the poles and 17 km up in the tropics.

TQV.label: Water vapour in the air column
TQV.simple: All the water vapour above a spot, from the ground to the top of the atmosphere — the millimetres of water you would get if it all rained out at once.

TQV.label: Water vapour in the air column

links.text: Air temperature and Surface temperature leave their norm in the same months, the same way: 113 times, where chance at the same moment of the record would give 80 (p = 3e-07; z = 6.7 against the same reading with one of them moved 1 to 5 years, beyond the shared trend and the persistence of each). So often, both ways (69 % and 68 %), that Eva takes them for one dynamic seen through the identity: in 103 months one left its norm without the other.

story.text: Air temperature — Western Pacific warm pool: +0.21 °C per decade (95 % range +0.176 to +0.241). Significant rising trend: both tests agree at the 95 % level. Mann-Kendall p = 4e-16, t-test p = 4.1e-12. Eva's dynamics, read year by year: one steady dynamic from 1981 to 2025 (+0.21 per decade): no change of regime stands out from the year-to-year swings. Eva: Since 2011, 80 % of months came out higher than Eva's norm expected from their neighbours (50 % if nothing had changed): the dynamic has left the norm she learned in 1981–2010.

Surface temperature — Western Pacific warm pool: +0.21 °C per decade (95 % range +0.168 to +0.26). Significant rising trend: both tests agree at the 95 % level. Mann-Kendall p = 7.8e-11, t-test p = 3e-09. Eva's dynamics, read year by year: one steady dynamic from 1981 to 2025 (+0.21 per decade): no change of regime stands out from the year-to-year swings. Eva: Since 2011, 74 % of months came out higher than Eva's norm expected from their neighbours (50 % if nothing had changed): the dynamic has left the norm she learned in 1981–2010.

Tropopause temperature — Western Pacific warm pool: +0.02 °C per decade (95 % range -0.143 to +0.182). A rising tendency that is not significant (yet): it could be chance. Mann-Kendall p = 0.82, t-test p = 0.99. With this much natural variability, a trend of this size needs about 310 years of data to stand out (45 so far). Eva's dynamics, read year by year: one steady dynamic from 1981 to 2025 (-0.00139 per decade): no change of regime stands out from the year-to-year swings. Eva: Since 2011, months come out above Eva's expectation 54 % of the time: not clearly different from her 1981–2010 norm.

Water vapour in the air column — Western Pacific warm pool: +0.31 kg/m² per decade (95 % range -0.172 to +0.744). A rising tendency that is not significant (yet): it could be chance. Mann-Kendall p = 0.19, t-test p = 0.35. With this much natural variability, a trend of this size needs about 60 years of data to stand out (45 so far). Eva's dynamics, read year by year: one steady dynamic from 1981 to 2025 (+0.222 per decade): no change of regime stands out from the year-to-year swings. Eva: Since 2011, months come out above Eva's expectation 50 % of the time: not clearly different from her 1981–2010 norm.
